Materials and methods: The information was obtained by searching the scientific literature published between 1977 and 2022 on online databases (including PubMed, CNKI, SciFinder, and Web of Science) and other sources (such as the Chinese Pharmacopoeia 2020 edition, and Chinese herbal books). Introduction The genus Polygonatum belongs to a perennial herbaceous plant whose English name is King Solomon’s seal, and it belongs to the Asparagaceae family. There are about 79 species of Polygonatum in the globe, which are extensively distributed in the northern hemisphere. About 39 species are recorded growing in China [1]. The genus Polygonatum has long been valued for its medicinal, diet, and healthcare values, the rhizomes are medicinal portions [2]. Polygonatumi rhizoma and Polygonatumi odorati rhizoma belong to the genus Polygonatum and have been added to the “Chinese Pharmacopeia” (2020 edition) [3]. The genus Polygonatum contains polysaccharides, flavonoids, steroids, coumarins, and other chemical components [4]. As a medicinal plant, its dried rhizome has anti-aging, anti-oxidation, immune regulation, anti-inflammatory, and anti-cancer effects, and is clinically used to treat fatigue, weakness, diabetes, cough, and loss of appetite [5]. However, the unprocessed herbs in genus Polygonatum can irritate the throat, the raw rhizomes of Polygonatum Mill. are processed by repeated steaming and drying (nine times each) in order to reduce toxic components, and improve their primary functioning, taste, and pharmaceutical effects [6]. Abstract Polygonatum sibiricum polysaccharides (PSPs) have attracted increasing attention due to their diverse biological activities and broad therapeutic potential. This review is presented as a comprehensive narrative review, based on a structured analysis of peer-reviewed literature published between 2000 and 2025, sourced from databases including PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus. It summarizes recent advances in the structural characterization, extraction technologies, and bioactivities of PSPs based on both in vitro and in vivo studies. Various extraction methods such as hot water extraction, ultrasound-assisted extraction, enzyme-assisted extraction (using cellulase and papain), radiation-assisted extraction, and green solvents like natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESs) and CO₂-triggered hydrophilic solvents are critically compared. Quantitative data from optimized conditions show PSP yields ranging from 4.4 % (hot water) to 29.7 % (NADES-based extraction). Structural features including monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkages, and molecular weight distribution are discussed in relation to pharmacological functions. PSPs demonstrate promising antioxidant, immunomodulatory, anti-diabetic, anti-obesity, hepatoprotective, and anti-tumoral effects. Clinical relevance is supported by evidence of improved immune response, glucose regulation, and lipid metabolism in preclinical disease models. Furthermore, PSPs hold potential for applications in the pharmaceutical, nutraceutical, and functional food industries due to their biocompatibility and therapeutic value. In conclusion, this review highlights the need for standardized extraction protocols, deeper investigations into structure activity relationships, and translational clinical research to advance the biomedical and industrial applications of PSPs. Introduction Polygonatum sibiricum (PS), commonly known as Siberian Solomon's Seal, is a recognized member of the Liliaceae family and has been traditionally valued for its dual culinary and medicinal uses, particularly in East Asia. Among its many bioactive components, polysaccharides are considered the primary pharmacologically important constituents and have attracted significant attention due to their diverse physiological and therapeutic functions, including immunomodulatory, antioxidant, hypoglycemic, and anti-inflammatory effects (Li et al., 2025). Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) extensively utilizes P. sibiricum, with its various components serving multiple therapeutic roles. The plant is rich in biologically active compounds such as lignans, vitamins, anthraquinones, polysaccharides, alkaloids, steroids, cardiac glycosides, and organic acids (Cui et al., 2018). Among these, polysaccharides stand out due to their high efficacy and low toxicity profile, making them ideal candidates for use in health supplements and functional foods. Compared to other plant-derived substances, polysaccharides are generally regarded as safe, biocompatible, and suitable for long-term use. An expanding body of literature highlights the pharmacological advantages of P. sibiricum polysaccharides (PSP), which exhibit a broad spectrum of bioactivities, including hypoglycemic (Chang et al., 2024), immunoregulatory (Chen et al., 2024a, Chen et al., 2024b), antioxidant (Wang et al., 2022), anti-osteoarthritic (Kuang et al., 2024), anti-cancer (Huang et al., 2020), and antidepressant effects (Zhang et al., 2023a, Zhang et al., 2023b). These characteristics have significantly broadened PSP’s applications in medicine, food sciences, and biotechnology (Li et al., 2025). The rhizomes of Polygonatum species have been utilized in traditional remedies for centuries due to their rich composition of polysaccharides, saponins, flavonoids, alkaloids, and lectins. Their therapeutic potential extends across a wide range of conditions, including fatty liver, Alzheimer’s disease, diabetes, cancer, cardiovascular dysfunction, and bone disorders (Zhao et al., 2018). Methods used to extract and characterize polysaccharides from Polygonatum

The available evidence indicates that Polygonatum polysaccharide extraction is not monolithic but varies by protocol and analytical approach. The most commonly reported methods include hot water extraction (HWE), alkaline extraction, ultrasonic-assisted extraction (UAE), enzyme-assisted extraction, and more recently green solvents such as natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESs) and CO₂-triggered hydrophilic solvents [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. One source also describes a traditional hot water extraction procedure using a Soxhlet extractor and boiling water bath, which is typical for polysaccharide isolation [N2-R1]. Another source explicitly states that hot water extraction is conventional because it offers high recovery rates and enhanced yield [N2-R3]. These methods differ in their effect on yield and purity: hot water can provide high recovery, but other methods such as UAE and enzyme-assisted extraction may improve yield further under optimized conditions [N2-R2][N2-R3]. However, the evidence here is largely methodological rather than comparative, so it supports the idea that standardized protocols matter for reproducibility and purity, but it does not provide a single “best” method across all Polygonatum species [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4].

For monosaccharide composition, the evidence points to HPLC-based methods with derivatization as the dominant analytical tool. A study reports the use of PABA-HPLC-FLD for determination of monosaccharide content in Polygonatum sibiricum and Polygonatum odoratum, and notes that this method is sensitive and suitable for compositional analysis [N3-R2]. Another study uses UHPLC–QTRAP–MS/MS to determine six monosaccharides in a Polygonatum sample, showing that modern hyphenated mass spectrometry can identify and quantify sugars with high specificity [N3-R1]. A third source describes hydrolysis followed by PMP derivatization and HPLC analysis, which is also a standard route for monosaccharide characterization [N3-R5]. These methods are complementary: HPLC-FLD and UHPLC–MS/MS are useful for relative quantification and identification, while derivatization and hydrolysis are needed to break down polysaccharides into individual monosaccharides for analysis [N3-R2][N3-R1][N3-R5].

For structural characterization, the evidence is broader. The review material notes that structural features include monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkages, and molecular weight distribution [N4-F2]. Another source reports that molecular weight is closely associated with functional characteristics and biological activity, making its determination a critical part of characterization [N5-R1]. It also reports that a polysaccharide from Polygonatum sibiricum had a molecular weight of 3.06 kDa, mainly composed of fructose and glucose in a 93.81:5.12 molar ratio [N5-R3]. Another source describes molecular weights of 2–5 kDa for Polygonatum cyrtonema Hua polysaccharides, and notes that low molecular weight is a common feature among these polysaccharides [N5-R4]. The evidence therefore shows that characterization extends beyond sugar composition to include linkage patterns and molecular weight, but the available excerpts do not provide enough detail to establish a standard structural fingerprint across species [N4-F2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4].

The limitations or biases introduced by method choice are clear in the evidence. First, different extraction methods can affect yield and purity; hot water is conventional but not necessarily the highest-yielding method, and UAE/NADES-based approaches may optimize yield under specific conditions [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. Second, analytical methods differ in sensitivity and specificity: PABA-HPLC-FLD is sensitive but may not capture all sugars equally, while UHPLC–MS/MS can provide more detailed identification [N3-R2][N3-R1]. Third, hydrolysis and derivatization can alter or obscure natural linkage information, and molecular weight determination is affected by the chosen chromatographic and analytical conditions [N3-R5][N5-R1]. Finally, the evidence does not establish a single method as unbiased; it instead implies that method choice is a variable that can influence the observed composition and structure [N2-R2][N3-R2][N5-R1][N5-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a methodological framework in which extraction protocols shape yield and purity, while analytical techniques such as HPLC and hyphenated mass spectrometry shape the ability to measure monosaccharide composition and structural features. The limitations are method-dependent: extraction bias, analytical sensitivity, and the effects of hydrolysis and derivatization all contribute to variation in results [N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-R2][N3-R5][N5-R1][N5-R4].

The empirical evidence in the provided materials indicates that Polygonatum polysaccharides commonly contain glucose, fructose, galactose, mannose, rhamnose, arabinose, xylose, and sometimes glucuronic acid or galacturonic acid. The most explicitly named monosaccharides come from the review material, which states that Polygonatum sibiricum polysaccharides (PSP) are composed of nine major monosaccharides: xylose, mannose, glucose, galactose, rhamnose, arabinose, glucuronic acid, galacturonic acid, and fructose [N4-F2]. Another source reports six monosaccharides in a Polygonatum sample: glucose, mannose, rhamnose, galactose, ribose, and arabinose [N3-R1]. A third source explicitly reports mannose, glucose, galactose, and arabinose in processed Polygonatum odoratum polysaccharides [N3-R3]. A fourth source notes that polysaccharides from Polygonatum sibiricum were mainly composed of fructose and glucose in a 93.81:5.12 molar ratio, with the rest of the composition not fully detailed in the excerpt [N5-R3]. These examples show that the common sugars are glucose, fructose, galactose, mannose, rhamnose, arabinose, xylose, and occasionally glucuronic acid/galacturonic acid [N3-R1][N3-R3][N4-F2][N5-R3].

The evidence also supports the idea that compositional variation is real but unevenly documented. The review explicitly states that Polygonatum species produce structurally diverse polysaccharides that vary in composition [N4-R1][N4-F2]. It also reports that 17 polysaccharides have been isolated from P. sibiricum, 16 from P. odoratum, 17 from P. cyrtonema, and 5 from P. kingianum, which suggests that multiple species have been studied, but the number of isolates is not directly comparable to compositional similarity [N6-R1]. The same review notes that PSPs mainly contain several types of polysaccharides, including fructan, pectin, galactomannan, glucomannan, arabinogalactan, and others, indicating that composition is not limited to a single sugar profile [N6-R4]. However, the excerpt does not provide direct comparisons of sugar proportions across species, so the variation is inferred rather than quantified.

The evidence is more explicit about differences among reported species in a limited sense. One study reports that a polysaccharide from P. kingianum consisted of Fru, Glc, and Gal and was characterized by a linear backbone with β-D-Fruf-(2 → 6)-β-D-Glc-(1 → 3)-β-D-Glc linkages [N6-R2]. This is a direct compositional statement for P. kingianum, but it is not directly compared with P. sibiricum or P. odoratum in the excerpt. Another study compares extraction rates, structure composition, and antioxidant capacity of PsP between young and mature rhizomes of P. sibiricum, which suggests that tissue maturity can affect composition, but not species comparison [N6-R3]. Whether compositional variation is consistent or context-dependent is supported by the evidence. The review states that Polygonatum polysaccharides vary in composition, implying that variation is not uniform across species [N4-R1][N4-F2]. It also notes that molecular weight is closely associated with functional characteristics and biological activity, and that PSPs demonstrate antioxidant, immunomodulatory, anti-diabetic, anti-obesity, hepatoprotective, and anti-tumoral effects [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. These effects are likely linked to composition, but the evidence does not show whether composition is consistent across species or changes with tissue, extraction, or analytical method. The most direct implication from the available material is that compositional variation is real and species-related, but the evidence is still limited by thin direct comparisons and by the fact that some variation may reflect tissue maturity or extraction conditions rather than species identity itself [N4-R1][N4-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

The evidence also supports the idea that compositional variation is real and species-related, but it is unevenly documented. The review material states that compositional variation is a hallmark of Polygonatum polysaccharides [N4-R1][N4-F2]. It also notes that molecular weight is closely associated with functional characteristics and biological activity, and that PSPs demonstrate antioxidant, immunomodulatory, anti-diabetic, anti-obesity, hepatoprotective, and anti-tumoral effects [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. The evidence indicates that there is direct comparison-level or at least review-level evidence for **P. sibiricum**, **P. kingianum**, **P. odoratum**, and **P. cyrtonema**, but the comparisons are uneven. The review explicitly states that Polygonatum species, including P. sibiricum, P. cyrtonema, P. kingianum, and P. odoratum, produce structurally diverse polysaccharides that vary in composition [N4-R1][N4-F2]. It also reports that 17 polysaccharides have been isolated from P. sibiricum, 16 from P. odoratum, 17 from P. cyrtonema, and 5 from P. kingianum, which shows these species have been studied intensively [N6-R1]. A separate source reports a novel polysaccharide from P. kingianum composed of Fru, Glc, and Gal with a linear backbone and specific glycosidic linkages [N6-R2]. For P. sibiricum, the evidence reports that one isolate was mainly composed of fructose and glucose in a 93.81:5.12 molar ratio [N5-R3], and that PSPs mainly contain several polysaccharide types [N6-R4]. For P. odoratum, the evidence includes PABA-HPLC-FLD analysis and the presence of mannose, glucose, galactose, and arabinose in processed polysaccharides [N3-R2][N3-R3]. For P. cyrtonema, the evidence notes that its polysaccharides are part of the structurally diverse group, but the excerpt does not provide a direct monosaccharide composition [N4-F2][N5-R4].

### 5) What confounding factors affect interpretation?

Several confounding factors make direct cross-species comparisons difficult to interpret. First, **tissue maturity** is a factor: a study compares young and mature rhizomes of P. sibiricum and reports differences in extraction rate, structure composition, and antioxidant capacity [N6-R3]. Second, **extraction method** matters because different protocols can affect yield and purity; the evidence shows that hot water extraction, UAE, enzyme-assisted extraction, and NADES-based methods are all used, with optimized conditions yielding different recovery rates [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. ### 6) Bottom line: how do the monosaccharide compositions vary?

Based on the evidence, the answer is:

- **Yes, they vary.** The review explicitly states that Polygonatum species produce structurally diverse polysaccharides that vary in composition [N4-R1][N4-F2]. 
- **But the variation is uneven.** Some species are reported more fully than others, and direct cross-species comparisons are limited [N4-R1][N4-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].
- **The most commonly detected sugars are glucose, fructose, galactose, mannose, rhamnose, arabinose, xylose, and sometimes glucuronic acid/galacturonic acid.** These are the sugars most consistently reported across the evidence [N4-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N5-R3].

Methods used to extract and characterize polysaccharides from Polygonatum

The available evidence indicates that Polygonatum polysaccharide extraction is not monolithic but varies by protocol and analytical approach. The most commonly reported methods include hot water extraction (HWE), alkaline extraction, ultrasonic-assisted extraction (UAE), enzyme-assisted extraction, and more recently green solvents such as natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESs) and CO₂-triggered hydrophilic solvents [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. One source also describes a traditional hot water extraction procedure using a Soxhlet extractor and boiling water bath, which is typical for polysaccharide isolation [N2-R1]. Another source explicitly states that hot water extraction is conventional because it offers high recovery rates and enhanced yield [N2-R3]. These methods differ in their effect on yield and purity: hot water can provide high recovery, but other methods such as UAE and enzyme-assisted extraction may improve yield further under optimized conditions [N2-R2][N2-R3]. However, the evidence here is largely methodological rather than comparative, so it supports the idea that standardized protocols matter for reproducibility and purity, but it does not provide a single “best” method across all Polygonatum species [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4].

For monosaccharide composition, the evidence points to HPLC-based methods with derivatization as the dominant analytical tool. A study reports the use of PABA-HPLC-FLD for determination of monosaccharide content in Polygonatum sibiricum and Polygonatum odoratum, and notes that this method is sensitive and suitable for compositional analysis [N3-R2]. Another study uses UHPLC–QTRAP–MS/MS to determine six monosaccharides in a Polygonatum sample, showing that modern hyphenated mass spectrometry can identify and quantify sugars with high specificity [N3-R1]. A third source describes hydrolysis followed by PMP derivatization and HPLC analysis, which is also a standard route for monosaccharide characterization [N3-R5]. These methods are complementary: HPLC-FLD and UHPLC–MS/MS are useful for relative quantification and identification, while derivatization and hydrolysis are needed to break down polysaccharides into individual monosaccharides for analysis [N3-R2][N3-R1][N3-R5].

For structural characterization, the evidence is broader. The review material notes that structural features include monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkages, and molecular weight distribution [N4-F2]. Another source reports that molecular weight is closely associated with functional characteristics and biological activity, making its determination a critical part of characterization [N5-R1]. It also reports that a polysaccharide from Polygonatum sibiricum had a molecular weight of 3.06 kDa, mainly composed of fructose and glucose in a 93.81:5.12 molar ratio [N5-R3]. Another source describes molecular weights of 2–5 kDa for Polygonatum cyrtonema Hua polysaccharides, and notes that low molecular weight is a common feature among these polysaccharides [N5-R4]. The evidence therefore shows that characterization extends beyond sugar composition to include linkage patterns and molecular weight, but the available excerpts do not provide enough detail to establish a standard structural fingerprint across species [N4-F2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4].

The limitations or biases introduced by method choice are clear in the evidence. First, different extraction methods can affect yield and purity; hot water is conventional but not necessarily the highest-yielding method, and UAE/NADES-based approaches may optimize yield under specific conditions [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. Second, analytical methods differ in sensitivity and specificity: PABA-HPLC-FLD is sensitive but may not capture all sugars equally, while UHPLC–MS/MS can provide more detailed identification [N3-R2][N3-R1]. Third, hydrolysis and derivatization can alter or obscure natural linkage information, and molecular weight determination is affected by the chosen chromatographic and analytical conditions [N3-R5][N5-R1]. Finally, the evidence does not establish a single method as unbiased; it instead implies that method choice is a variable that can influence the observed composition and structure [N2-R2][N3-R2][N5-R1][N5-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a methodological framework in which extraction protocols shape yield and purity, while analytical techniques such as HPLC and hyphenated mass spectrometry shape the ability to measure monosaccharide composition and structural features. The limitations are method-dependent: extraction bias, analytical sensitivity, and the effects of hydrolysis and derivatization all contribute to variation in results [N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-R2][N3-R5][N5-R1][N5-R4].

Methods used to extract and characterize polysaccharides from Polygonatum

The available evidence indicates that Polygonatum polysaccharide extraction is not monolithic but varies by protocol and analytical approach. The most commonly reported methods include hot water extraction (HWE), alkaline extraction, ultrasonic-assisted extraction (UAE), enzyme-assisted extraction, and more recently green solvents such as natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESs) and CO₂-triggered hydrophilic solvents [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. One source also describes a traditional hot water extraction procedure using a Soxhlet extractor and boiling water bath, which is typical for polysaccharide isolation [N2-R1]. Another source explicitly states that hot water extraction is conventional because it offers high recovery rates and enhanced yield [N2-R3]. These methods differ in their effect on yield and purity: hot water can provide high recovery, but other methods such as UAE and enzyme-assisted extraction may improve yield further under optimized conditions [N2-R2][N2-R3]. However, the evidence here is largely methodological rather than comparative, so it supports the idea that standardized protocols matter for reproducibility and purity, but it does not provide a single “best” method across all Polygonatum species [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4].

For monosaccharide composition, the evidence points to HPLC-based methods with derivatization as the dominant analytical tool. A study reports the use of PABA-HPLC-FLD for determination of monosaccharide content in Polygonatum sibiricum and Polygonatum odoratum, and notes that this method is sensitive and suitable for compositional analysis [N3-R2]. Another study uses UHPLC–QTRAP–MS/MS to determine six monosaccharides in a Polygonatum sample, showing that modern hyphenated mass spectrometry can identify and quantify sugars with high specificity [N3-R1]. A third source describes hydrolysis followed by PMP derivatization and HPLC analysis, which is also a standard route for monosaccharide characterization [N3-R5]. These methods are complementary: HPLC-FLD and UHPLC–MS/MS are useful for relative quantification and identification, while derivatization and hydrolysis are needed to break down polysaccharides into individual monosaccharides for analysis [N3-R2][N3-R1][N3-R5].

For structural characterization, the evidence is broader. The review material notes that structural features include monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkages, and molecular weight distribution [N4-F2]. Another source reports that molecular weight is closely associated with functional characteristics and biological activity, making its determination a critical part of characterization [N5-R1]. It also reports that a polysaccharide from Polygonatum sibiricum had a molecular weight of 3.06 kDa, mainly composed of fructose and glucose in a 93.81:5.12 molar ratio [N5-R3]. Another source describes molecular weights of 2–5 kDa for Polygonatum cyrtonema Hua polysaccharides, and notes that low molecular weight is a common feature among these polysaccharides [N5-R4]. The evidence therefore shows that characterization extends beyond sugar composition to include linkage patterns and molecular weight, but the available excerpts do not provide enough detail to establish a standard structural fingerprint across species [N4-F2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4].

The limitations or biases introduced by method choice are clear in the evidence. First, different extraction methods can affect yield and purity; hot water is conventional but not necessarily the highest-yielding method, and UAE/NADES-based approaches may optimize yield under specific conditions [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. Second, analytical methods differ in sensitivity and specificity: PABA-HPLC-FLD is sensitive but may not capture all sugars equally, while UHPLC–MS/MS can provide more detailed identification [N3-R2][N3-R1]. Third, hydrolysis and derivatization can alter or obscure natural linkage information, and molecular weight determination is affected by the chosen chromatographic and analytical conditions [N3-R5][N5-R1]. Finally, the evidence does not establish a single method as unbiased; it instead implies that method choice is a variable that can influence the observed composition and structure [N2-R2][N3-R2][N5-R1][N5-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a methodological framework in which extraction protocols shape yield and purity, while analytical techniques such as HPLC and hyphenated mass spectrometry shape the ability to measure monosaccharide composition and structural features. The limitations are method-dependent: extraction bias, analytical sensitivity, and the effects of hydrolysis and derivatization all contribute to variation in results [N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-R2][N3-R5][N5-R1][N5-R4].

Empirical evidence of monosaccharide composition variation across species

The empirical evidence in the provided materials indicates that Polygonatum polysaccharides commonly contain glucose, fructose, galactose, mannose, rhamnose, arabinose, xylose, and sometimes glucuronic acid or galacturonic acid. The most explicitly named monosaccharides come from the review material, which states that Polygonatum sibiricum polysaccharides (PSP) are composed of nine major monosaccharides: xylose, mannose, glucose, galactose, rhamnose, arabinose, glucuronic acid, galacturonic acid, and fructose [N4-F2]. Another source reports six monosaccharides in a Polygonatum sample: glucose, mannose, rhamnose, galactose, ribose, and arabinose [N3-R1]. A third source explicitly reports mannose, glucose, galactose, and arabinose in processed Polygonatum odoratum polysaccharides [N3-R3]. A fourth source notes that polysaccharides from Polygonatum sibiricum were mainly composed of fructose and glucose in a 93.81:5.12 molar ratio, with the rest of the composition not fully detailed in the excerpt [N5-R3]. These examples show that the common sugars are glucose, fructose, galactose, mannose, rhamnose, arabinose, xylose, and occasionally glucuronic acid/galacturonic acid [N3-R1][N3-R3][N4-F2][N5-R3].

The evidence also supports the idea that compositional variation is real but unevenly documented. The review explicitly states that Polygonatum species produce structurally diverse polysaccharides that vary in composition [N4-R1][N4-F2]. It also reports that 17 polysaccharides have been isolated from P. sibiricum, 16 from P. odoratum, 17 from P. cyrtonema, and 5 from P. kingianum, which suggests that multiple species have been studied, but the number of isolates is not directly comparable to compositional similarity [N6-R1]. The same review notes that PSPs mainly contain several types of polysaccharides, including fructan, pectin, galactomannan, glucomannan, arabinogalactan, and others, indicating that composition is not limited to a single sugar profile [N6-R4]. However, the excerpt does not provide direct comparisons of sugar proportions across species, so the variation is inferred rather than quantified.

The evidence is more explicit about differences among reported species in a limited sense. One study reports that a polysaccharide from P. kingianum consisted of Fru, Glc, and Gal and was characterized by a linear backbone with β-D-Fruf-(2 → 6)-β-D-Glc-(1 → 3)-β-D-Glc linkages [N6-R2]. This is a direct compositional statement for P. kingianum, but it is not directly compared with P. sibiricum or P. odoratum in the excerpt. Another study compares extraction rates, structure composition, and antioxidant capacity of PsP between young and mature rhizomes of P. sibiricum, which suggests that tissue maturity can affect composition, but not species comparison [N6-R3]. In addition, a source reports that P. sibiricum extract contained four times more phenolic components than P. odoratum extract, though this is not a monosaccharide comparison and is likely unrelated to polysaccharide composition [N6-R5]. Therefore, the evidence supports compositional variation across species, but it is strongest for P. kingianum and weakest for direct cross-species comparisons [N4-R1][N4-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

Whether compositional variation is consistent or context-dependent is supported by the evidence. The review states that Polygonatum polysaccharides vary in composition, implying that variation is not uniform across species [N4-R1][N4-F2]. It also notes that molecular weight is closely associated with functional characteristics and biological activity, and that PSPs demonstrate antioxidant, immunomodulatory, anti-diabetic, anti-obesity, hepatoprotective, and anti-tumoral effects [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. These effects are likely linked to composition, but the evidence does not show whether composition is consistent across species or changes with tissue, extraction, or analytical method. The most direct implication from the available material is that compositional variation is real and species-related, but the evidence is still limited by thin direct comparisons and by the fact that some variation may reflect tissue maturity or extraction conditions rather than species identity itself [N4-R1][N4-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

Species-specific taxonomy and polysaccharide-relevant biology

The evidence indicates that the Polygonatum genus is large and taxonomically diverse, with 79 species globally and about 39 species in China [N1-F1]. The genus is classified in the Asparagaceae family, and Polygonatum species are perennial herbaceous plants with rhizomes used as functional foods and medicinal materials [N1-F1][N1-R2]. This taxonomic context is important because it explains why species comparisons are meaningful: the genus is not a single taxon, and different species may differ in composition, chemistry, and ecological adaptation.

Among the most commonly studied species in the provided evidence are Polygonatum sibiricum, Polygonatum cyrtonema, Polygonatum kingianum, and Polygonatum odoratum [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-F2][N6-R1]. These species are repeatedly cited as targets of research and as examples of structural diversity in Polygonatum polysaccharides [N4-R1][N4-F2]. Polygonatum sibiricum is especially prominent in the review literature; it is described as a species belonging to the Polygonatum genus and as a key focus of recent reviews on structural insights, bioactivities, and therapeutic potential [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-F2]. Polygonatum odoratum is also heavily represented in the evidence, with studies on its polysaccharide extraction, composition, and antioxidant potential [N1-F1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R5]. Polygonatum cyrtonema is mentioned as a species producing structurally diverse polysaccharides and as one of the species in the genus whose polysaccharides are the focus of comparative research [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-F2]. Polygonatum kingianum is reported as one of the species whose polysaccharides have been isolated and characterized [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2]. Taken together, these four species are the most commonly studied in the provided evidence, with P. sibiricum and P. odoratum appearing most frequently as the center of compositional and structural studies [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-F2][N6-R1][N6-R5].

The commonly reported polysaccharide-rich parts or tissues are the rhizomes. The evidence repeatedly notes that Polygonatum rhizomes are the medicinal portions used in traditional remedies, and that polysaccharides, saponins, flavonoids, alkaloids, and lectins are present in them [N1-F1]. It also states that the rhizomes have been used in traditional remedies for centuries because they are rich in polysaccharides and other bioactive compounds [N1-F1]. In addition, one source explicitly states that the rhizomes of Polygonatum species have been utilized in traditional remedies for centuries due to their rich composition of polysaccharides, saponins, flavonoids, alkaloids, and lectins [N5-R5]. Another review notes that the rhizomes are the medicinal portion and that the dried rhizome is clinically used to treat fatigue, weakness, diabetes, cough, and loss of appetite [N1-F1]. These statements indicate that rhizomes are the primary tissue studied for polysaccharides, rather than leaves, flowers, or other organs.

The biological context that may influence composition is also present in the evidence. First, habitat and ecological distribution are implied by the taxonomic context: Polygonatum species are distributed across the northern hemisphere, and about 39 species are recorded in China [N1-F1]. Second, processing changes are emphasized as affecting chemical constituents and pharmacological effects. The review states that many chemical constituents and pharmacological activities change after unappropriated processing, and that raw rhizomes may irritate the throat, so repeated steaming and drying are used to reduce toxic components and improve pharmaceutical effects [N1-F1]. This suggests that post-harvest processing can alter composition and bioavailability, which is relevant to polysaccharide studies because processing may affect yield, purity, and structural integrity. Third, the evidence notes that the same species can vary in composition depending on tissue maturity: a study compares young and mature rhizomes of P. sibiricum and reports differences in extraction rate, structure composition, and antioxidant capacity [N6-R3]. This supports the idea that composition is not fixed within a species but may depend on developmental stage or tissue maturity. The evidence does not provide explicit genotype-by-environment comparisons, so the biological context remains mainly taxonomic, tissue-related, and processing-related [N1-F1][N1-R2][N5-R5][N6-R3].

The review also states that PSPs are composed of nine major monosaccharides, including xylose, mannose, glucose, galactose, rhamnose, arabinose, glucuronic acid, galacturonic acid, and fructose [N4-F2]. In summary, the evidence supports direct comparison-level studies or review-level evidence for P. sibiricum, P. kingianum, P. odoratum, and P. cyrtonema, but the comparisons are uneven and often indirect. Methods used to extract and characterize polysaccharides from Polygonatum

The available evidence indicates that Polygonatum polysaccharide extraction is not monolithic but varies by protocol and analytical approach. The most commonly reported methods include hot water extraction (HWE), alkaline extraction, ultrasonic-assisted extraction (UAE), enzyme-assisted extraction, and more recently green solvents such as natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESs) and CO₂-triggered hydrophilic solvents [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. One source also describes a traditional hot water extraction procedure using a Soxhlet extractor and boiling water bath, which is typical for polysaccharide isolation [N2-R1]. Another source explicitly states that hot water extraction is conventional because it offers high recovery rates and enhanced yield [N2-R3]. These methods differ in their effect on yield and purity: hot water can provide high recovery, but other methods such as UAE and enzyme-assisted extraction may improve yield further under optimized conditions [N2-R2][N2-R3]. However, the evidence here is largely methodological rather than comparative, so it supports the idea that standardized protocols matter for reproducibility and purity, but it does not provide a single “best” method across all Polygonatum species [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4].

For monosaccharide composition, the evidence points to HPLC-based methods with derivatization as the dominant analytical tool. A study reports the use of PABA-HPLC-FLD for determination of monosaccharide content in Polygonatum sibiricum and Polygonatum odoratum, and notes that this method is sensitive and suitable for compositional analysis [N3-R2]. Another study uses UHPLC–QTRAP–MS/MS to determine six monosaccharides in a Polygonatum sample, showing that modern hyphenated mass spectrometry can identify and quantify sugars with high specificity [N3-R1]. A third source describes hydrolysis followed by PMP derivatization and HPLC analysis, which is also a standard route for monosaccharide characterization [N3-R5]. These methods are complementary: HPLC-FLD and UHPLC–MS/MS are useful for relative quantification and identification, while derivatization and hydrolysis are needed to break down polysaccharides into individual monosaccharides for analysis [N3-R2][N3-R1][N3-R5].

For structural characterization, the evidence is broader. The review material notes that structural features include monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkages, and molecular weight distribution [N4-F2]. Another source reports that molecular weight is closely associated with functional characteristics and biological activity, making its determination a critical part of characterization [N5-R1]. It also reports that a polysaccharide from Polygonatum sibiricum had a molecular weight of 3.06 kDa, mainly composed of fructose and glucose in a 93.81:5.12 molar ratio [N5-R3]. Another source describes molecular weights of 2–5 kDa for Polygonatum cyrtonema Hua polysaccharides, and notes that low molecular weight is a common feature among these polysaccharides [N5-R4]. The evidence therefore shows that characterization extends beyond sugar composition to include linkage patterns and molecular weight, but the available excerpts do not provide enough detail to establish a standard structural fingerprint across species [N4-F2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4].

The limitations or biases introduced by method choice are clear in the evidence. First, different extraction methods can affect yield and purity; hot water is conventional but not necessarily the highest-yielding method, and UAE/NADES-based approaches may optimize yield under specific conditions [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. Second, analytical methods differ in sensitivity and specificity: PABA-HPLC-FLD is sensitive but may not capture all sugars equally, while UHPLC–MS/MS can provide more detailed identification [N3-R2][N3-R1]. Third, hydrolysis and derivatization can alter or obscure natural linkage information, and molecular weight determination is affected by the chosen chromatographic and analytical conditions [N3-R5][N5-R1]. Finally, the evidence does not establish a single method as unbiased; it instead implies that method choice is a variable that can influence the observed composition and structure [N2-R2][N3-R2][N5-R1][N5-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a methodological framework in which extraction protocols shape yield and purity, while analytical techniques such as HPLC and hyphenated mass spectrometry shape the ability to measure monosaccharide composition and structural features. The limitations are method-dependent: extraction bias, analytical sensitivity, and the effects of hydrolysis and derivatization all contribute to variation in results [N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-R2][N3-R5][N5-R1][N5-R4].

The evidence also supports the idea that compositional variation is real but unevenly documented. The review explicitly states that Polygonatum species produce structurally diverse polysaccharides that vary in composition [N4-R1][N4-F2]. The same review notes that PSPs mainly contain several types of polysaccharides, including fructan, pectin, galactomannan, glucomannan, arabinogalactan, and others, indicating that composition is not limited to a single sugar profile [N6-R4]. The evidence is more explicit about differences among reported species in a limited sense. Whether compositional variation is consistent or context-dependent is supported by the evidence.
